source.title: You don't need error nodes, you need better features

record.file_problem: The full post is present, but some equations and symbols are missing or garbled in the web text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse-autoencoder feature recovery to Gemma-2-2B and reports reconstruction measurements, an LLM setting rather than the original toy-model setting. It does not test superposition geometry directly.
record.gate_note: The post discusses the superposition hypothesis, but reports no tests of feature overlap, near-orthogonality, importance-dependent geometry, neuron polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality. Included rows are the Table 13 single-layer RRE measurements, which bear on whether sparse dictionaries recover activations. Replacement-model KL, benchmark, and validity results concern the utility of replacement models rather than the claim versions' feature properties, so they are not rows here.
record.test_reason: An SAE engineering post on Gemma-2-2B. It assumes the superposition hypothesis (Appendix C) and uses SAEs as a tool. It reports only its own methods' performance (KL, benchmarks, RRE) against standard SAEs and Gemma Scope. No result bears on whether features are superposed, polysemantic, recoverable as genuine sparse features, canonical, or 1-D. The RRE values have no non-sparse or random baseline that could show sparse structure exists.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author argues error nodes are unnecessary if SAEs are made robust to upstream error. Replacement-aware training, encoder tuning and LISTA encoders sharply cut replacement-model KL without hurting full-replacement RRE. MMLU accuracy stays at or below chance unless QA fine-tuning and debiasing are added. Superposition is assumed as background, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The original source concerns toy networks and feature geometry; this post trains sparse autoencoders for residual-stream replacement models in Gemma-2-2B and measures reconstruction and end-to-end replacement performance.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported single-layer RRE varies with SAE training method and encoder configuration; the post also reports layer-dependent changes in reconstruction comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: In full replacement models, excess reconstruction error over single-layer RRE grows roughly as the square root of layer depth. Replacement-aware training and LISTA encoders trade worse single-layer RRE for slower compounding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE re-encoding error compounds across layers in full replacement models, and training objectives can trade single-layer fidelity for robustness.

record.problems: Results concern one base model, Gemma-2-2B. No uncertainty estimates are reported, and the author notes that the implementation and hyperparameters may be suboptimal. Reconstruction metrics do not establish that the recovered features are semantically genuine or canonical.
record.rows_left_out: The post reports many layer-by-layer RRE values in Tables 8–11 and additional replacement-model KL and benchmark results. They are omitted because Table 13 supplies summary single-layer RRE values for the tested SAE configurations, while the other measures do not directly test V4's feature-recovery claim.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: no analysis of capacity competition or neuron polysemanticity.
Whether LLM activations contain recoverable sparse features. RRE is reported only to compare SAE training methods, with no baseline that could show sparse structure.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not measured. The post shows feature choice depends on training objective, but reports no feature-level comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and its V4 supports/limits_scope labels are not justified. RRE values here compare SAE training recipes and do not bear on whether superposition or recoverable sparse features exist. The only engagement with superposition is a conceptual framing in Appendix C.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity or gives important features dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
Tests SAE reconstruction of activations in Gemma-2-2B, but not whether features are semantically genuine, how features distribute across neurons, or whether the result generalizes to other LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The study reports single-layer RRE for sparse autoencoders and treats reconstruction as a measure of faithfulness, providing evidence of activation recovery (rows r1–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported RREs are nonzero, and the post describes SAE re-encoding as lossy; these results do not establish recovery of semantically genuine, complete, or canonical features (rows r1–r9).
